module_title: Grounds for Eviction: The Battlefield of Landlord vs. Tenant
introduction: This intermediate tier dissects the actual grounds on which a landlord can legally throw a tenant out. It focuses heavily on Section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control (DRC) Act, 1958, which serves as the blueprint for almost all state judiciary exams (UP, MP, Rajasthan).

core_concepts.title: Ground 1: Non-Payment of Rent (Sec 14(1)(a) DRC Act)
core_concepts.description:
A landlord cannot just evict a tenant the day they miss a payment.
- The Process: The landlord must serve a formal legal notice of demand. The tenant is given **two months** to pay the arrears. 
- The Savior Clause: If it is the tenant's *first* default, the Rent Controller will give them one final chance to pay the arrears (usually within 1 month). If they pay, the eviction is blocked. However, if they default a second time (three consecutive months), they get no second chance and are evicted.

core_concepts.title: Ground 2: Bona Fide Requirement (Sec 14(1)(e) DRC Act)
core_concepts.description:
The most fiercely litigated ground for eviction.
- The Rule: The landlord requires the premises *bona fide* (in good faith, not as a trick) for their own residence or for any member of their family dependent on them.
- The Strict Conditions: To win, the landlord MUST prove: (1) They are the absolute owner, (2) The requirement is genuine and pressing (not a mere 'desire' or whim), and (3) They have **no other reasonably suitable alternative accommodation** in the city.

core_concepts.title: Ground 3: Sub-letting (Sec 14(1)(b) DRC Act)
core_concepts.description:
When the tenant becomes a mini-landlord.
- The Rule: A tenant cannot sub-let, assign, or part with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the **consent in writing** of the landlord. Oral consent is legally meaningless in court. If proven, this leads to immediate eviction.

core_concepts.title: Ground 4: Material Alteration & Nuisance
core_concepts.description:
- Material Alteration: If the tenant builds a permanent structure or fundamentally alters the premises without written consent, causing damage to the property's value or utility.
- Nuisance: If the tenant is using the premises for illegal/immoral purposes or is causing a severe nuisance to the neighbors (e.g., turning a quiet residential flat into a noisy factory).

important_entities.name: Leave and License Agreement (Maharashtra Context)
important_entities.key_fact: The corporate loophole to avoid Rent Control.
important_entities.significance: Under the Maharashtra Rent Control Act, a formal 'Lease' grants tenancy rights that are hard to terminate. To bypass this, owners in Mumbai exclusively use 'Leave and License' agreements (governed by the Indian Easements Act). A license merely grants *permission* to use the premises, does not transfer an interest in the property, and allows for swift eviction upon expiry.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Historically, in Delhi, a landlord could only evict a tenant for bona fide requirement if the premises were let for *residential* purposes. However, in the landmark case of **Satyawati Sharma v. Union of India (2008)**, the Supreme Court struck down this distinction as unconstitutional. Now, a landlord can evict a tenant from a *commercial* shop for their bona fide requirement as well.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: To succeed in an eviction suit under Section 14(1)(e), the landlord must prove these three absolute elements.

exam_strategy_tips: In Judiciary Mains, when drafting an eviction judgment based on Non-Payment of Rent, you MUST mention whether the mandatory **two-month notice** was served, as failure to serve it makes the eviction petition instantly void.
